newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China seen undermining future HK government.
newsitem.headline: China seen undermining future HK government.

text.p: An influential pro-Beijing politician has warned that Chinese plans to station an official with the rank of minister in post-colonial Hong Kong might undermine the territory's future government.

Professor Lau Siu-kai told the South China Morning Post newspaper that the Xinhua News Agency, which serves as China's de facto embassy in Hong Kong, would overshadow future leader Tung Chee-hwa if accorded the status of a central government representative.

Xinhua deputy director Zhang Junsheng said last weekend that the agency would be headed by an official of ministerial rank, indicating its power would be geater than China's planned new Foreign Ministry mission, which will be headed by a commissioner with the rank of vice-minister.

The Xinhua office is the focus of speculation in Hong Kong that China's communist rulers will renege on promises to allow Hong Kong a high level of autonomy after Britain hands it back to Beijing on July 1.

Zhang and Xinhua director Zhou Nan, the most senior Communist Party officials in Hong Kong, have often sparred verbally with British governor Chris Patten and Hong Kong's Democratic Party over democracy and human rights.

A China-controlled committee named Tung last December as chief executive of Hong Kong after the British depart, but his work has already been overshadowed by policy pronouncements from Beijing leaders.

Lau, a member of the China-controlled Hong Kong handover Preparatory Committee, said handover documents did not provide for a central government agency in Hong Kong. He said such a body would inevitably get involved in political polemics.
"Some of the territory's political groups might turn to the agency as an avenue of appeal if their demands were rejected by the SAR government," Lau said.
"At worst, Xinhua could become the focus of forces against the chief executive.
"With its immense resources and connections the agency could also affect the configuration of political forces in post-1997 Hong Kong and even the selection of a future chief executive.
"It would give an impression that there was another authority appointed by Beijing other than Mr Tung," Lau said.
Last weekend, Zhang also said Xinhua would remain in place after the handover.
